messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Ingrid

Ingrid was seventy-eight when the hurricane came. She and her husband Martin had lived in their Charleston home for forty-three years—a restored Victorian with high ceilings and large windows that faced the harbor. She had designed the interiors herself, refinishing the woodwork, choosing the paint colors, hanging the art. It was hers in a way few things are. When the storm warning came, they evacuated as instructed, driving inland to a motel two hours away. Martin held her hand in the car. They expected to return to minor damage, perhaps some loose shingles. What they found instead was erasure. The surge had come through with such force that the first floor was gutted. The furniture they'd collected over decades was splintered and soaked. The photographs—all of them, going back to their children's births—were destroyed. The walls themselves were compromised, the plaster bloated and peeling. The house that had been the container of her identity for four decades was no longer a home. It was a ruin.

In the weeks after, Ingrid found herself unable to hold what had happened as something finished. The memory didn't sit in the past where it belonged; it felt present, immediate, as though the water were still rising around her ankles. When she tried to recall the moment she first saw the damage, the feeling was strange and hollow—she could recount the facts, the color of the water line on the walls, the smell of mold, but the details seemed to belong to someone else's story. The event was so extreme, so disproportionate to what she believed the world owed her, that her mind resisted it as real. This can't have actually happened, she would think, staring at photographs of the wreckage. Yet it had. And the more she tried to push the memory away, the more it refused to settle into the past where she could leave it behind.

The house itself became the trigger. But it wasn't just the house. When Martin opened the back door one morning last month, the sudden sound of it opening—that particular creak and slam—sent her heart racing. Doors opening meant the water was coming again. Talk of her neighbors who had lost family members in other disasters, or of distant relatives' misfortunes, would catch in her chest and pull her backward. Even the smell of alcohol on a stranger's breath at the grocery store could unsettle her, though she couldn't quite explain why—something about it, some association her mind had made without her permission. Each of these moments reminded her of something she had come to believe with absolute certainty: the world was not safe. Bad things happened randomly, without warning or justice. The life she had built could be stolen in an afternoon. Nothing she had done, no care she had taken, had protected her. Her beliefs about fairness, about cause and effect, about what she deserved at seventy-eight—all of it had been shattered like the windows of her house.

Because the world felt dangerous and unpredictable, Ingrid began to clean. She scrubbed the rental apartment where she and Martin now lived with an intensity that bordered on frantic. She organized and reorganized the boxes of salvaged items, the few things that had survived. If she could impose order on her immediate surroundings, if she could control what was in front of her, perhaps she could prevent another disaster. She also found herself turning the event over in her mind repeatedly, examining each decision she had made that day. If they had left earlier. If they had boarded up the windows differently. If they had purchased better insurance. The rumination gave her a grim sense of agency—if she could identify what she should have done, then perhaps she could ensure it never happened again. But the cleaning and the endless reconsideration of the past were also ways of not thinking about the memory itself, of keeping it at arm's length. Yet the more she scrubbed and reorganized and ruminated, the more vivid the memory became. The harder she tried to erase it, the more present it felt, as though the act of fighting it kept it alive in real time.

Martin had begun to withdraw. He sat in the living room of their rental and said little. Ingrid's compulsive organizing meant their new space was sterile, unwelcoming. Her rumination had turned into a kind of endless monologue that left no room for him. She had been a graphic designer for fifty years, and she had planned to work part-time in retirement, but she couldn't focus. A client had asked her to design a logo last month, and she had stared at the blank screen for hours, unable to think beyond the thought that nothing she created would last, that chaos could destroy it all at any moment. She hadn't taken another project since. The loss of that small creative outlet, the way her mind now rejected the possibility of building anything, was another consequence she hadn't anticipated. What frightened her most was that she couldn't stop the cycle—the more she tried to prevent another disaster through vigilance and control, the more trapped she felt in the memory of the first one. She had come to see the world as fundamentally unjust, and nothing she did seemed to change that conviction.
